'''''Dracaena sanderiana''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asparagaceae]], native to [[Central Africa]].<ref name=Damen18>{{cite journal|author=Damen, T.H.J.|title= Taxonomic novelties in African Dracaena (Dracaenaceae)|date= 2018|journal= Blumea Journal of Plant Taxonomy and Plant Geography|volume= 63| pages=31–53| url=http://www.repository.naturalis.nl/document/656937}}</ref> It was named after the German–English gardener [[Henry Frederick Conrad Sander]] (1847–1920). The plant is commonly [[marketed]] as "'''lucky bamboo'''," which has become one of its [[common name]]s, although it is not a species of [[bamboo]].

==Names==
Common names include '''Sander's dracaena''', '''ribbon dracaena''', '''lucky bamboo''', '''curly bamboo''', '''Chinese water bamboo''', '''Goddess of Mercy's plant''', '''Belgian evergreen'''.<ref>{{cite book | author = Hugh T. W. Tan and Xingli Giam | title = Plant Magic: Auspicious and Inauspicious Plants from Around the World | year = 2008 | publisher = Marshall Cavendish Editions|isbn = 9789812614278 | page = 62 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=CiBFAQAAIAAJ&q=%22ribbon-dracaena%22}}</ref> It is also called the '''ribbon plant''', although the same common name is sometimes used for ''[[Chlorophytum comosum]]'' (also known as the ''spider plant''). While the word ''bamboo'' occurs in several of this plant's common names, ''D. sanderiana'' is of an entirely different taxonomic [[Order (biology)|order]] from true [[Bambusoideae|bamboo]]s – though this plant and true bamboos both fall under the [[monocot]] [[clade]]. Despite several of its common names that suggest it is from China or Belgium, it is a native West African species.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dracaena sanderiana (Chinese Water Bamboo, Friendship Bamboo, Lucky Bamboo, Ribbon Plant, Water Bamboo) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/dracaena-sanderiana/ |access-date=2025-02-05 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> ''Dracaena sanderiana'' is also often confused with ''[[Dracaena braunii]]'', a plant from coastal West Africa with flowers 5 times shorter than those of ''D. sanderiana''.<ref name=Damen18/>

==Description==
A [[perennial plant|perennial]] herb reaching a height of {{convert|100|cm|abbr=on}}, the plant has slightly twisted, gray-green leaves which grow to around {{convert|23|cm|0|abbr=on}}. Its fleshy stem distinguishes it from [[bamboo]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Croft |first=August |date=2022-07-05 |title=Lucky Bamboo vs Bamboo: What's the Difference? |url=https://a-z-animals.com/blog/lucky-bamboo-vs-bamboo-whats-the-difference/ |access-date=2025-02-05 |website=A-Z Animals |language=en-US}}</ref> Over time, the plant's stem becomes unsteady with the added weight of new growth. Regular trimmings are needed to ensure the shape of this plant stays neat and manageable while it grows.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Charlie |date=2025-01-02 |title=How to Grow and Care for Lucky Bamboo Indoors - Plant Help |url=https://planthelp.me/wiki/how-to-grow-and-care-for-lucky-bamboo/ |access-date=2025-01-02 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
{{More citations needed|date=December 2024}}
{{how-to|date=January 2025}}
''Dracaena sanderiana'' and its related varieties are popular houseplants. It is a suitable plant for confined spaces, and it does very well in indirect sunlight or partial shade as direct sunlight often causes its leaves to burn or yellow.<ref name=":0" /> The ideal temperature range for ''D. sanderiana'' is from {{convert|16 to 27|C|F}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=How to Care for a Dracaena |url=https://www.thesill.com/blogs/plants-101/how-to-care-for-a-dracaena#:~:text=This%20plant%20likes%20bright,%20indirect,plant%20them%20indoors%20or%20outdoors. |access-date=2025-02-05 |website=The Sill |language=en}}</ref> It requires average warmth, adequate light, and regular watering with dry periods in between<ref name=":0" /> if planted in soil. It tolerates dry air, but because it is a tropical plant, it does best in higher humidity areas or when given regular mistings.<ref name=":0" /> When planted indoors, it stays a smaller, more compact size while growing upwards, leading to its bamboo-like appearance. In contrast, if planted in the ground, it loses its bamboo-like look and it would fill with a leaf-like shape like other [[dragon tree]]s. When it comes to light, lucky bamboo prefers bright, filtered sunlight, such as what is found under a '''rainforest''' canopy. Avoid direct sunlight as it will scorch the leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 28, 2024 |title=How to Grow and Care for Lucky Bamboo Indoors |url=https://medium.com/@spacewar/how-to-grow-and-care-for-lucky-bamboo-indoors-c22696800d6e |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241228180945/https://medium.com/@spacewar/how-to-grow-and-care-for-lucky-bamboo-indoors-c22696800d6e |archive-date=December 28, 2024 |website=medium.com}}</ref> It can be propagated by cutting a part of the stem just above a node (the "rings" around the plant's stem from which offshoots grow).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Miranda |first=Molly B. |date=2022-05-04 |title=How to Propagate Lucky Bamboo {{!}} Care Guide {{!}} HRC |url=https://houseplantresourcecenter.com/2022/05/how-to-propagate-lucky-bamboo-care-guide/ |access-date=2025-02-05 |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Cuttings (plant)|Cuttings]] can be made year round.
